title: Natural Carbon Sinks Absorb 40% of Human CO2 Emissions and Are Not Valued in Most Climate Models
gist: Wood Mackenzie's new report finds natural sinks (oceans, forests) absorb ~40% of the 48 GtCO2/year humans emit, dwarfing engineered removal (DAC/BECCS) by ~200,000x, yet these sinks are weakening, unpriced by carbon markets, and structurally assumed-stable in most net zero models — creating tail risk for climate policy and an early-mover opportunity in verified nature-based carbon instruments.

themes.theme: Natural sinks dwarf engineered carbon removal

insights.claim: In 2025, natural sinks (oceans ~12 GtCO2, forests ~6 GtCO2) absorbed roughly 18 GtCO2, cutting gross global human emissions of 48 GtCO2 down to net emissions of approximately 30 GtCO2 — about 40% of annual human CO2 output.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Net zero math implicitly relies on natural sink health as much as on emissions cuts — a systemic assumption most climate and portfolio models don't price.

insights.claim: Engineered carbon removal — direct air capture and bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) combined — removed only 0.08 GtCO2 in 2025, about 200,000 times less than annual CO2 uptake from oceans alone.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Engineered CDR remains a rounding error versus natural sinks today; near-term climate math still depends almost entirely on nature, not technology — tempers over-optimistic DAC/BECCS growth narratives.
insights.quote: Engineered removals, including direct air capture and bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), contributed only 0.08 GtCO2 in 2025, 200,000 times less than annual CO2 uptake from oceans.

insights.claim: Net human CO2 emissions have risen more than 80% since 1990, meaning growth in sink absorption has not kept pace with growth in emissions.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Watch whether sink capacity can decouple from the emissions growth trend — historically it has not.
insights.quote: Net CO2 emissions due to human activities have risen more than 80% since 1990.

themes.theme: Forests are flipping from carbon sink to carbon source

insights.claim: Global forest area has declined by 1.5 million km2 since 1990, with deforestation now contributing 5 to 6 GtCO2 of emissions annually.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Deforestation-linked supply chains (agriculture, timber, palm oil) face rising carbon-pricing and regulatory exposure as this trend is quantified.
insights.locator: Sinks are the unpriced foundation of climate targets

insights.claim: The land-use sector has had near-neutral net emissions since 2024, meaning it has effectively lost its historical role as a net carbon sink.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A previously 'free' climate buffer has disappeared, raising the burden on energy-sector decarbonization and engineered removals to hit net zero.
insights.quote: The land-use sector has had near-neutral net emissions since 2024, losing its role as a net sink.
insights.locator: Sinks are the unpriced foundation of climate targets

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's base-case scenario has global forest area continuing to contract through 2030, with only gradual recovery after that point.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Forest-linked carbon credits and reforestation-exposed assets face a multi-year headwind before base-case recovery even begins.
insights.locator: Sinks are the unpriced foundation of climate targets

insights.claim: Warming and forest sink loss reinforce each other in a feedback loop: higher temperatures drive more wildfires, which further reduce forests' absorption capacity.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Mental model explaining why sink degradation can accelerate nonlinearly rather than track emissions linearly — relevant for stress-testing net zero timelines.
insights.quote: Rising temperatures create a self-reinforcing feedback loop: greater warming results in more fires, which further reduces absorption.
insights.locator: Sinks are the unpriced foundation of climate targets

insights.claim: Canada's 2023 boreal wildfires alone released 3 GtCO2, converting that boreal forest region from a net carbon sink into a net emissions source — a real-world example of a tipping-point process already underway.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Shows tipping points are not theoretical: a single fire season can erase years of assumed sink capacity, a key risk for anyone underwriting forest-carbon-credit permanence.
insights.quote: Canada's 2023 boreal fires alone released 3 GtCO2, converting boreal forest from carbon sink to emission source.
insights.locator: Sinks are the unpriced foundation of climate targets

insights.claim: Protecting and restoring forests could deliver an additional 3 to 6 GtCO2 of mitigation annually.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Nature-based mitigation (avoided deforestation, restoration) is a large, currently underfinanced abatement opportunity roughly comparable in scale to current annual forest carbon uptake.
insights.locator: Sinks are the unpriced foundation of climate targets

themes.theme: Earth-system tipping points are a large, underpriced tail risk

insights.claim: Five major Earth system tipping points — permafrost thaw, Amazon dieback, boreal forest fires, coral reef die-off, and Atlantic Ocean circulation disruption — carry a combined potential greenhouse gas release exceeding 750 GtCO2, and some of these processes are already unfolding.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: This tail risk is equivalent to over 15 years of current gross global emissions and is not captured in most climate or financial risk models — a candidate for scenario/stress-test coverage.
insights.quote: Five major Earth system tipping points carry a combined greenhouse gas release potential exceeding 750 GtCO2.
insights.locator: Sinks are the unpriced foundation of climate targets

insights.claim: Coral reef die-off would disrupt fisheries that sustain over a billion people globally, linking ocean carbon-sink degradation to food security and coastal economies.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Second-order social and economic exposure for insurers, food companies, and coastal-economy-linked assets tied to ocean sink health.
insights.quote: Coral reef die-off would disrupt fisheries that sustain over a billion people globally.
insights.locator: Sinks are the unpriced foundation of climate targets

themes.theme: Net zero pathways structurally depend on sinks that aren't guaranteed

insights.claim: Even under Wood Mackenzie's net zero scenario (global net emissions reaching zero by 2050), about 11 GtCO2 of residual energy-sector emissions remain annually; under the country pledges scenario (net zero by 2060), that residual rises to around 14 GtCO2 — emissions that must still be absorbed by natural or engineered sinks.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Renewables deployment and efficiency gains alone cannot close the gap — sink health and engineered-removal scale-up are load-bearing, not optional, assumptions in every credible net zero pathway.
insights.quote: Approximately 11 GtCO₂ of emissions remain under the net zero scenario, where global net emissions reach zero by 2050, rising to around 14 GtCO₂ under the country pledges scenario, where net emissions reach zero by 2060.
insights.locator: Why the pace of renewables deployment cannot close the gap alone

themes.theme: Carbon markets misprice sink degradation — a policy and investment blind spot

insights.claim: Carbon prices in most compliance markets range from $5 to $90 per tCO2, levels the report says do not reflect the true cost of natural sink degradation; current policy frameworks price only emissions while treating natural sinks as free infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Current carbon price levels understate transition and physical risk; a repricing event (higher price floors, sink-linked instruments) is a plausible catalyst for compliance-market and offset-linked positions.
insights.quote: Current policy frameworks treat natural sinks as free infrastructure while pricing only emissions, a structural blind spot in climate policy.
insights.locator: Why the pace of renewables deployment cannot close the gap alone

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's scenario analysis identifies 2026 to 2035 as the decisive window, with sink trajectories diverging sharply depending on the policy and finance action taken during this period.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Near-term, this-decade policy and financing decisions — not 2050 targets — are the key variable to monitor for sink-related investment risk and opportunity.
insights.quote: The 2026 to 2035 window is decisive: scenario analysis shows sink trajectories diverge sharply based on action taken now.
insights.locator: Why the pace of renewables deployment cannot close the gap alone

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie senior analyst Roshna Nazar argues ecosystem collapse is permanent on human timescales, unlike the energy transition which can still accelerate in later years, and that early movers in verified nature-based solutions and sink-linked carbon instruments will capture value as demand scales and regulation tightens.
insights.speaker: Roshna Nazar
insights.so_what: Direct investment framing: position early in verified nature-based carbon credits and sink-linked instruments ahead of anticipated demand growth and regulatory tightening.
insights.quote: Unlike the energy transition, which can accelerate in later years, ecosystem collapse is permanent on human timescales. Each decade of inaction removes future optionality.

insights.claim: Regions with weak environmental enforcement today are likely to face abrupt policy tightening once sink losses become visible, creating sudden compliance burdens for exposed assets.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Flags regulatory-surprise risk for companies and assets in jurisdictions with currently lax land-use or carbon enforcement — a compliance and legal risk watch item.
insights.quote: Regions with weak enforcement today are likely to face abrupt policy tightening as sink losses become visible, creating sudden compliance burdens for exposed assets.
